sources.entry: Why books don’t work, Andy Matuschak.

summary.title: Why books don't work
summary.one_liner: Books, like lectures, rest on an implicit and flawed "transmissionism" model of learning, so readers often absorb far less than they think, and better learning media need to be designed around explicit cognitive models.
takeaways: Readers often feel they understood a non-fiction book until someone asks a probing question, revealing they absorbed only a few sentences.
Books and lectures share an implicit transmissionist model: knowledge passes directly from words on a page to the reader, which learning science considers false.
Effective reading requires heavy metacognition (self-questioning, monitoring, feedback), which static books leave largely to the reader.
Textbooks use explicit cognitive models with exercises, but still shift most metacognitive work onto readers; courses add scheduling, feedback, discussion, and emotional salience.
The author proposes designing new media built on explicit cognitive models rather than trying only to fix the traditional book form.
summary.summary: The essay argues that explanatory non-fiction books often fail to transmit the knowledge their authors intend, and that readers mostly don't notice. It draws a parallel with lectures: both media implicitly assume transmissionism, the idea that understanding passes straight from words to the listener or reader. The author explains that effective reading demands metacognitive skill and self-monitoring that books cannot respond to, and compares textbooks and courses, noting that courses offer feedback, social discussion, accountability, and emotional engagement. The piece concludes that the goal should be designing new media grounded in explicit cognitive models, rather than only improving books.
